output.query: aneurysmal SAH management Hunt-Hess WFNS Fisher coiling clipping

results.finding: The Hunt and Hess scale grades the clinical severity of aneurysmal SAH from I to V and correlates with surgical risk and outcome.
The amount and distribution of subarachnoid blood on the admission CT predicts later vasospasm.
Surgical or endovascular treatment of the ruptured aneurysm should be performed as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset; early enteral nimodipine improves outcome.
In ruptured aneurysms suitable for both techniques, endovascular coiling gave a higher rate of independent survival at one year than neurosurgical clipping.

output.summary: Clinical grade (Hunt and Hess, WFNS) and CT blood burden (Fisher) stratify outcome and vasospasm risk. Guidelines recommend securing the ruptured aneurysm as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours, and early enteral nimodipine. Where an aneurysm suits both techniques, coiling was associated with better one-year independent survival than clipping.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture before non-contrast CT in suspected SAH.
Do not perform lumbar puncture when CT already confirms SAH with mass effect, intraventricular hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus — herniation risk.
Do not start aspirin or other antiplatelet agents before the aneurysm is secured — increases rebleeding risk.
Do not inject the contents of nimodipine capsules intravenously or by any other parenteral route (risk of cardiovascular collapse); give nimodipine enterally.
Do not give NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, ketorolac) for headache control before aneurysm securing — antiplatelet effect raises rebleeding risk.
Do not pursue cardiac catheterization for neurogenic troponin elevation without strong primary-ACS evidence — delays aneurysm treatment.
Do not leave severe hypertension untreated before the aneurysm is secured, and do not lower blood pressure to the point of hypotension.
required_recommendations: Initiate non-contrast CT head as the first diagnostic step in suspected SAH; do not delay for other workup.
Obtain CT angiography of the head and neck immediately after positive non-contrast CT to characterize the aneurysm.

Start enteral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours (orally or by nasogastric tube) as soon as aneurysmal SAH is confirmed and continue for 21 days; if it causes hypotension, give 30 mg every 2 hours rather than stopping it [Hoh_2023].

Arrange urgent joint neurosurgical and neurointerventional review and secure the ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm by endovascular coiling or microsurgical clipping as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset [Hoh_2023]; the technique is chosen jointly from the aneurysm anatomy and the patient's condition.
Admit to a neurocritical care unit at a centre with neurosurgical and neurointerventional capability, with hourly neurological checks and continuous cardiac monitoring.

Lower blood pressure now with a short-acting titratable intravenous agent (nicardipine or clevidipine infusion, or labetalol boluses) until the aneurysm is secured, avoiding hypotension; the 2023 guideline sets no numeric target [Hoh_2023] and systolic pressure below 160 mmHg is the commonly used target [Connolly_2012].
Withhold amlodipine while on nimodipine (additive dihydropyridine effect).
Monitor serum sodium closely for cerebral salt wasting / SIADH and avoid hypotonic fluids.

Monitor for delayed cerebral ischemia from day 3 to day 14 with frequent neurological examinations, with transcranial Doppler surveillance as a reasonable adjunct; maintain euvolemia and do not use prophylactic hypervolemia [Hoh_2023].

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is not part of standard SAH workup; reserve for evaluation of unexplained altered mental status suggesting non-convulsive status epilepticus.
EMG/NCS has no role in acute SAH evaluation or management.
Sleep study is irrelevant to acute SAH workup.

accepted: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from anterior communicating artery aneurysm (Hunt-Hess 2, Fisher 3)

differential.key_features: Thunderclap onset, and the exertional trigger, overlap with SAH; RCVS gives convexity SAH and segmental vasoconstriction, whereas this case shows basal-cistern blood and a saccular anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CTA.
Headache and neck pain overlap; CTA of the neck shows no dissection.
Sudden headache overlaps; no sellar mass or hemorrhage on CT and no visual field or ocular motor deficit.
Headache overlaps; no hyperdense sinus or venous infarct on CT, and the aneurysmal SAH explains the presentation.
Excluded by subarachnoid blood on CT.

key_clinical_evidence: Sudden, peak-in-seconds 'thunderclap' headache is SAH until proven otherwise — peak intensity ≤1 minute is the highest-yield historical feature.

Non-contrast CT is close to 100% sensitive within 6 hours of onset on a modern scanner read by an experienced radiologist; sensitivity falls after 6 hours and markedly by days 5 to 7, and anemia lowers it, so a negative CT does not exclude SAH in late presenters.

After a negative CT, lumbar puncture is indicated when the patient presents more than 6 hours after onset or has a new neurological deficit; spectrophotometric bilirubin needs about 12 hours to form and persists for about two weeks or longer.
Distinguish SAH from traumatic LP using non-clearing RBC counts across tubes 1-4 and xanthochromia (absent in traumatic).
Once SAH is confirmed, CT angiography of the head and neck characterizes the aneurysm and drives the clipping-versus-coiling decision.
Hunt-Hess and WFNS grades stratify clinical severity and outcome; modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm risk from CT blood distribution.
Neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo pattern, troponin elevation, T-wave inversions, QTc prolongation) is common in SAH and should not divert attention to a primary cardiac workup.

Nimodipine 60 mg PO every 4 hours for 21 days is the only proven pharmacologic prophylaxis for delayed cerebral ischemia in aneurysmal SAH — it does not prevent angiographic vasospasm but improves outcomes.
Securing the ruptured aneurysm by coiling or clipping as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset, reduces rebleeding, which carries high mortality.
Delayed cerebral ischemia occurs mainly between days 3 and 14; frequent neurological examination is the core of surveillance and transcranial Doppler is a reasonable adjunct.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Catecholamine surge from acute SAH causes neurogenic myocardial injury (Takotsubo physiology) in up to 30-40% of patients; echocardiogram showing apical ballooning confirms etiology and the focus remains on aneurysm securing.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Cardiac biomarker rise plus ST/T-wave changes may anchor the workup toward a primary acute coronary syndrome and a cardiology-first pathway.

patient.chief_complaint: Worst headache of life while exercising at gym, vomiting, neck stiffness
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Thompson is a 54-year-old woman with hypertension and active smoking who presents to the emergency department. She was on the elliptical machine at the gym when she developed an instantaneous, explosive headache she rates as 10/10, unlike anything she has experienced before. She immediately vomited, dropped to the ground, and was helped by gym staff who called 911. She remained conscious throughout. On EMS arrival, her blood pressure was 198/116 mmHg. She arrives with severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and one additional vomiting episode en route. She has no prior history of severe headaches. She denies focal weakness, vision loss, or loss of consciousness. Her history includes hypertension, smoking, and a family history of aneurysm. Hunt-Hess Grade 2 on arrival.
